In situ protein–protein interaction assays further confirmed the modulatory activity of selected compounds, identifying, to our knowledge, the first small-molecule enhancers of the NCS-1/cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1R) interaction. CB1R is an attractive pharmacological target implicated in neuronal signaling, whose activity is regulated by NCS-1. High-resolution crystal structures revealed how these modulators engage the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice, providing structural insights into ligand recognition and suggesting a mechanism of action. These findings connect generative molecular design with experimentally accessible NCS-1 ligands and provide chemical tools and structural insights for investigating NCS-1-dependent regulation of CB1R.

item.title: Measuring the Membrane Protein-Bound Lipidome
item.description: Lipids play diverse physiological roles in energy storage, signaling, and cell structure. Another less appreciated role is as allosteric modulators of membrane proteins. However, it is challenging to determine the identify and affinity of lipids interacting with a given membrane protein target. In this review, we discuss analytical advances in using lipidomics to profile lipids bound to specific membrane proteins, which we will refer to as protein-lipid interactomics. We will consider the challenges of solubilizing and isolating the membrane protein while retaining relevant lipid interactions, focusing on detergents and lipid nanoparticles made with polymer, peptide, and protein scaffolds. We will also discuss aspects of overall experiment design, including basic identification, quantitative experiments, progressive delipidation, and lipid exchange to probe the strength of lipid interactions. Finally, we conclude with key questions, current analytical challenges, and proposed future directions for this emerging field.

item.title: Analytic Hessian for mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory
item.description: Mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory (MRSF-TDDFT) describes diradicals and nearly degenerate states largely free of the spin contamination of spin-flip (SF) TDDFT, but its Hessian has been available only numerically. Within the Tamm–Dancoff approximation, we derive and implement the analytic Hessian of MRSF-TDDFT with restricted open-shell references, including SF-TDDFT as a special case, and the analytic polarizability derivative for excited-state Raman intensities. For stilbene, the analytic Hessian reproduces finite-difference frequencies to within 0.07 cm⁻¹ at one-nineteenth of the estimated three-point finite-difference cost. The Hessians show that the twisted S₁ intermediate (the phantom state) is an MRSF minimum and characterize the diradical S₀ saddle point. Computed ¹³C isotope shifts are consistent with the assignment of the S₁ resonance Raman band of the central C=C bond; at the phantom state, this band lies about 170 cm⁻¹ lower than at the planar S₁ minimum, a candidate marker of the twist. At the saddle point, SF-TDDFT gives energies and a reaction-coordinate curvature close to those of MRSF-TDDFT, but in a direction orthogonal to the reaction coordinate its Hessian has an unphysical mode at 6005 cm⁻¹ and, at a nearby point on the path, an imaginary frequency of 3358i cm⁻¹. S₀ and the MS = 0 component of T₁ are roots of the same SF response matrix; spin contamination couples them in the Hessian through a term inversely proportional to their gap. MRSF-TDDFT, with separate singlet and triplet response matrices, has no such term. Spin contamination can thus affect curvatures much more than energies.

item.title: Ultrathin high-aspect-ratio chiral gold nanofibers
item.description: Chirality, a fundamental characteristic of nature, plays a decisive role in molecular recognition, catalysis, and cellular organization. Translating this asymmetry into synthetic systems has the potential to unlock new functionalities at the interface of nanoscience and biology. Here, we report the synthesis of high-aspect-ratio chiral gold nanofibers, a class of one-dimensional chiral plasmonic materials, fabricated via a seedless, ligand-assisted growth method using D/L-cysteine as chiral inducers. The growth mechanism seems to involve initial particle and aggregate formation, the emergence of short filaments associated with these domains, and subsequent elongation and interconnection into nanofibers. Surfactant attachment onto the particle surface may have facilitated anisotropic growth within this pathway, but their organization and any restructuring during synthesis cannot be established. The resulting chiral gold nanofibers exhibit pronounced, mirror-symmetric circular dichroism signals and characteristic plasmonic resonances, confirming their intrinsic structural chirality. Further, 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy analysis indicates areas of the nanofibers with continuous variations of the crystal orientation, which can be linked to the observed topographical chirality of the gold nanofibers. Altogether, this effort establishes a simple and scalable route to fabricate chiral gold architectures with potential applications in asymmetric catalysis, optical sensing and bio-instructive scaffoldings.

item.title: The Hg + O → HgO Reaction on the Triplet Potential Energy Surface: A CCSD(T)/VTST Investigation
item.description: The gas-phase reaction of atomic mercury (Hg) with ground-state atomic oxygen (O(3P)) is relevant to mercury oxidation in combustion flue gases and non-thermal plasma environments. However, no experimental rate constants for this reaction are available in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Chemical Kinetics Database. Here, the reaction is investigated using density functional theory at the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/SDD+6-311++G(3df,3pd) level, combined with CCSD(T) single-point energy calculations. A relaxed potential energy surface (PES) scan was performed along the Hg–O coordinate from 1.80 to 10.00 Å on the spin-free triplet surface. Within this range, the calculated potential energy decreases as the atoms approach, and no entrance-channel barrier above the separated-reactant energy is observed at the sampled points. The equilibrium Hg–O bond length is 2.14 Å, and the dissociation energy D0 is 7.54 kcal mol-1. Variational RRKM calculations using generalized transition states yield a rate constant of 6.47 × 10-10 cm3 molecule-1 s-1 at 300 K, with weak temperature dependence over 300–500 K. The calculated rate constants are compared with Wilcox’s forward association rate expression, accounting for differences in electronic-state descriptions and kinetic treatments. These results provide kinetic data for the Hg + O reaction at low temperatures and a basis for evaluating the atomic-oxygen pathway in mercury oxidation models relevant to non-thermal plasma applications.

item.title: Side-Reaction Pathways and Catalyst Deactivation during ATRP of N-Vinylpyrrolidone
item.description: The atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) of N-vinylpyrrolidone (NVP) remains challenging due to the low activation of the vinyl group and the prevalence of competing side reactions. In this work, we systematically investigated the polymerization of NVP using alkyl bromide initiators and Cu(Me6Cyclam)Br-based catalysts under a range of solvent environments and monomer concentrations. 1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H-NMR) kinetic studies revealed extensive monomer consumption through competing pathways, including hydrolysis, dimerization, and solvent-mediated addition reactions, which significantly suppressed productive propagation. Several reaction intermediates and by-products were identified and structurally characterized, including the previously proposed compound 1,1-bis-(N-2-oxopyrrolidinyl)ethane, which was isolated and confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and multidimensional NMR spectroscopy. Comparative solvent studies showed that protic and polar media promote acid-catalyzed transformations of NVP, likely triggered by in situ generation of HBr through halide displacement from the copper catalyst. Increasing monomer concentration partially favored propagation but did not eliminate competing reactions. To circumvent these limitations, a PLA-based macroinitiator strategy was employed, enabling the synthesis of amphiphilic PVP-b-PLA diblock copolymers with improved polymerisation efficiency. Mechanistic analysis suggests that propagation suppression arises from a combination of catalyst deactivation, solvent-mediated halide displacement, and acid-catalyzed side reactions that consume monomer. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the complex reactivity of Nvinylpyrrolidone under ATRP conditions and highlight key factors limiting controlled radical polymerization of low-activated vinyl amide monomers.

item.title: Mechanistic Determinants of Passive Permeation in Binary Lipid Membranes from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description: Passive permeation is a fundamental determinant of pharmacokinetics. The models that simulate permeation pathways and predict their energetic requirements need to account for the complexity of biological membranes. However, the impact of lipid bilayer composition on the thermodynamics of the passive permeation process is not yet fully understood. This study systematically evaluates how specific lipid types influence the free energy profiles through binary lipid bilayers for six xenobiotics with structural diversity: amantadine, diclofenac, metoprolol, pindolol, ranitidine, and scopolamine. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted using MemCross, an all-atom MD protocol based on the Accelerated Weight Histogram (AWH) method, for five binary lipid mixtures. The bilayer models combined 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) with cholesterol (CHOL), 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (POPE), 1,2-diarachidonoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DAPC), or N-stearoyl-D-erythro-sphingosylphosphorylcholine (SM18) to represent the lipid diversity of human plasma cell membranes. Our results demonstrate the lipid features that significantly modulate the free energy landscapes. Permeation appeared governed jointly by lipid composition and the intrinsic molecular properties of the permeants. We identify a series of mechanistic descriptors that drive the permeation process, explaining how they collectively contribute to passive permeation outcomes. Based on this knowledge, multivariate models were established, identifying key descriptors that can be obtained from rapid non-biased MD simulations.

item.title: FLAMES – A flexible and extensible code for Monte Carlo simulations of nanoporous materials
item.description: Molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations are the cornerstone for computational studies of adsorption in nanoporous materials such as zeolites, Metal-Organic Frameworks, and Covalent Organic Frameworks. Currently, most of these simulations rely on classical force fields, which are often limited in their ability to describe specific interactions or the intrinsic flexibility of the host framework. Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a powerful alternative, offering near ab initio accuracy while remaining computationally feasible, potentially capturing framework flexibility and complex potential energy surfaces. Despite this promise, there is a significant gap, as current tools implementing MLIPs are often general-purpose codes adapted for adsorption or in-house solutions. Here, we introduce FLAMES (Flexible Lattice Adsorption by Monte Carlo Engine Simulation), a new software package designed to perform Monte Carlo-based simulations of nanoporous materials using MLIPs and other energy calculation methods, paving the way for more accurate and physically realistic molecular simulations. We detailed the implementation of different methodologies, including Widom insertion, Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC), hybrid GCMC/MD, and Transition Matrix Monte Carlo simulations, presenting validation examples for each method and evaluating the performance and accuracy of different energy calculation methodologies.

item.title: Pre-training on Quantum Mechanical Properties Improves ADMET Prediction
Intermediate Precision of Single-Molecule Break-Junction Conductance: Measurement, Uncertainty Budget, and Design Rules
item.description: A break-junction experiment reports a molecule’s conductance from thousands of junctions recorded in one session, with an uncertainty computed from those same junctions. That uncertainty describes one session. It does not say how much the value would change if the experiment were repeated on another day with a new tip, substrate and solution. We measure this change on archived recordings of DNA:RNA duplexes that include repeat sessions at identical settings. Across seven pairs of sessions, the session-to-session standard deviation of the median conductance is a factor of 1.46 (95% interval 1.28 to 2.15), 6.4 times the usual error bar. Five ways of removing it, each tested under pre-registration, did not work. A value from a single session therefore carries an expanded uncertainty of a factor of 2.4. Spreading the same number of traces over more sessions reduces it, and we give the number of sessions a comparison needs. Public data from a second laboratory show the same effect.

item.title: Unlocking Nb2O5 for Thermocatalytic CO2 Hydrogenation via Mutual Reconstruction across Metal-Niobia Interfaces
item.description: Thermocatalytic CO2 hydrogenation could efficiently take place at the interfaces between transition metals and reducible oxides, such as CeO2, TiO2, ZrO2, and In2O3, whose oxygen vacancies play catalytic roles in adsorbing and activating CO2. In contrast, Nb2O5 has not been widely recognized as a functional oxide to facilitate CO2 activation when interfaced with transition metals. In this study, we show that the reduction of several transition metal/Nb2O5 catalysts unlocks the CO2 activation activity of Nb2O5, demonstrating considerable higher activity towards CO2 hydrogenation than their Nb-free counterparts. Most notably, the Rh/Nb2O5 interface, supported on SBA-15, shows the most profound promotional effect for CO2 methanation relative to Nb-free 2Rh/SBA-15 catalyst. At 200 °C, the optimized 2Rh5Nb/SBA-15 catalyst affords 37.2- and 13.3-fold increases in specific reaction rate and turnover frequency, respectively, relative to Nb-free 2Rh/SBA-15. Spectroscopic characterizations and density functional theory calculations suggest that during catalyst pre-reduction in H2, interfacial hydrogen transfer from Rh promotes the formation of defect-rich NbOx. The reduced NbOx in turn facilitates extensive electronic interaction with Rh, resulting in the formation of dispersed Rhδ+ species and abundant Rhδ⁺-Ov-Nb4+ interfacial ensembles. These interfacial ensembles represent highly active centers for CO2 methanation through a COOH-mediated pathway, with CO2 activation on regenerable oxygen vacancies playing a key role in the catalytic cycle, while the strongly adsorbed CO* limits the subsequent hydrogenation via CO. The present findings establish transition metal/NbOx interface as a new structural platform for designing metal-oxide catalysts for hydrogenation and deoxygenation reactions, while expanding material space for designing robust CO2 hydrogenation catalysts beyond the existing library of reducible oxides.

item.title: Using potential derivatives to reduce the cost of rectangular collocation: a general and versatile approach for computational vibrational spectroscopy without a potential energy surface
item.description: We modify the exact Cartesian kinetic energy operator, rectangular collocation approach of Manzhos and Carrington [J. Chem. Phys. 145 (2016) 224110] by using information contained in potential derivatives to decrease the number of required potential points. We show that this makes it possible to substantially reduce the number of collocation points, which is important, in particular, when energies are computed directly ab initio. Vibrational band intensities are also computed. We first demonstrate the method on Cl2CO and compare to high-accuracy Smolyak collocation calculations on an accurate potential energy surface (PES). Sub-cm-1 accuracy is obtained with a few thousand Gaussian basis functions and potential points. A spectrum computed directly from DFT energies and a comparison to GVPT2 (generalized vibrational perturbation theory) are also presented. We then consider LiCO2 as a more anharmonic case, for which a quartic force field potential is less reliable, and which also serves as a surrogate model for a catalytic system (mimicking CO2 bond weakening by charge donation). The rectangular collocation method is used to compute the spectrum of LiCO2 directly from ab initio energies and to compare to GVPT2. The method is implemented as a Claude Skill and is easily usable by anyone on any molecule. The method is a general and versatile tool for anharmonic computational vibrational spectroscopy. It does not require a PES and no coupling is neglected.

item.title: Sustained Radiopacity of Biodegradable Iodinated Polyether Blends for Tracking Long-Term Degradation in Medical Devices
item.description: Longitudinal monitoring of biomedical devices is emerging as the next phase of personalized medicine, enabling individualized treatment plans based on radiological evaluation of devices over time. However, incorporation of a contrast agent is necessary to functionalize polymeric devices for imaging, but must be balanced by changes in device properties and biocompatibility. Here we demonstrate the use of a novel polymer blend as a potential material for biomedical devices incorporating imaging functionality, consisting of 90% biodegradable poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA 50:50) matrix and 10% of an iodinated block co-polymer, poly(ethylene oxide)-co-poly(epichlorohydrin) (PEO-PECH). Addition of the iodinated PEOPECH produced porous radiopaque phantom devices with up to 3 wt% iodine. The porous phantoms remained CT-visible for the duration of a 12-week in vitro degradation study, with changes in attenuation correlating to changes in apparent density. Phantom mechanics and mass loss were affected by PECH molecular weight and iodine content in the blend but remained comparable to properties of clinical devices. During degradation, iodine was released from phantoms at a steady rate. The iodine remained molecularly bound to the polyether, which was lost more slowly than the PLGA matrix. The stable degradation and consistent attenuation make this blend promising for use in biomedical devices.

item.title: Recipes for a Broad, Low-Barrier AI Bootcamp in Chemistry
item.description: Artificial intelligence literacy is becoming an important component of chemical education and workforce preparation as AI transforms chemical research and professional practice. In the late summer of 2026, we organized a 30-hour AI bootcamp for the incoming graduate students in chemistry, biochemistry, and the broader community. Here, we discuss the main goals and design principles of the event and summarize several teaching modules that can be combined to design AI bootcamps of different lengths and scopes. Unlike a formal course on the topic, our core intention was to provide multiple starting points for the participants to self-explore and adopt AI tools for their own learning and research without requiring specialized knowledge of mathematics or computer programming. Key lessons included the strong dependence of outcomes on students’ AI literacy and model choice, the value of hands-on and discussion-based activities, and the need for a modular curriculum that can be updated rapidly as AI tools evolve.

item.title: Biomolecular Recognition Programs Fusion and Segregation of Orthogonal DNA Condensates
item.description: Controlling interactions between synthetic compartments is essential for building responsive, reconfigurable molecular systems. Here, we demonstrate that biomolecular recognition programs the fusion of orthogonal DNA-based condensates. To do that, we re-engineered ligand-functionalized DNA nanostars whose orthogonal sticky-end interactions drive phase separation into initially immiscible condensate populations. Addition of a bridging bivalent protein introduces heterotypic connections that promote condensate association, coalescence, and mixing. Through proteolytic cleavage of the biomolecular receptor, we can then restore segregation of the condensate populations. We demonstrate this approach using antigen-functionalized nanostars, with IgG antibodies inducing fusion and papain triggering segregation. We then extend the approach to thrombin-mediated fusion of condensates displaying aptamers for distinct thrombin exosites, followed by trypsintriggered segregation. A mean-field model coupled to phase-field dynamics reproduces the observed morphologies and suggests competition between antigen recognition and neighboring sticky-end bonding as a possible mechanism allowing efficient mixing. These results establish biomolecular recognition as a modular means of dynamically rewiring the composition and connectivity of synthetic compartments without redesigning the DNA interactions that drive their initial formation.

item.title: Marine Exopolysaccharide Diabolican Enhances the Physical Properties of Collagen Hydrogels via a Temperature-Dependent Polyionic Complexation
item.description: Collagens and glycosaminoglycans are essential components of the extracellular matrix, providing key biochemical and mechanical properties. Type I collagen and hyaluronan (HA) are therefore widely used in tissue engineering to mimic the characteristics of human tissues. However, native HA does not significantly improve the properties of collagen hydrogels when combined with this biopolymer. In this study, the marine exopolysaccharide diabolican (HE800 strain), which exhibits structural similarities to HA, was evaluated as an alternative glycosaminoglycan for combination with type I collagen. Mixing collagen with diabolican led to the formation of polyionic complexes (PICs), even under conditions of high osmotic strength. Complex formation depended on both the molecular weight of diabolican and temperature. Performing the mixing on ice slowed down complexation, enabling the preparation of homogeneous hydrogels. The interplay between PIC formation and collagen gelation generated composite hydrogels with significantly improved physical properties when high-molecular-weight (HMW) diabolican was used, doubling the mechanical strength compared to pure collagen. Encapsulated fibroblasts remained viable, adopted a spindle shaped morphology, proliferated, and did not induce hydrogel contraction until day seven. Importantly, these advantages were achieved without chemical functionalization or crosslinking. Overall, HMW diabolican represents a promising alternative to hyaluronan for tissue engineering applications.

item.title: A shared formulation design space reveals poly(2-ethyl-2oxazoline) chain length as a determinant of lipid nanoparticle performance and relative organ distribution
item.description: The interface between lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and their biological environment represents a key determinant of biodistribution. Here, we investigated poly(2-ethyl-2oxazoline) (PEtOx)-lipids as an adaptable component of this interface and determined how polymer chain length affects LNP formulation as well as biological behavior. Rather than comparing different polymers with a single nominal formulation composition, we first mapped the pharmaceutical design space of four PEtOx-lipids containing average chain lengths of 20, 34, 49, or 71 repeating units and identified formulation conditions that supported acceptable LNP formation. This shared design space subsequently enabled the comparison of chain-length-dependent effects under pharmaceutically viable conditions. Increasing PEtOx chain length decreased the apparent hydrophobicity of the PEtOx-lipids and was associated with progressively smaller LNP diameters, lower mRNA encapsulation efficiencies, and a narrower formulation space in which predefined criteria for size, polydispersity, and mRNA loading were met concomitantly. Optimized PEtOx-LNPs mediated mRNA expression across multiple primary and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cell types with limited effects on cell viability. Pooled in vivo DNA barcoding of the PEtOx20-, PEtOx34-, and PEtOx49-LNPs revealed chain-length-dependent differences in relative organ barcode distribution, with shorter chains shifting relative distribution toward spleen and pancreas and away from bone marrow and liver. Together, these findings establish PEtOx chain length as an independent LNP design parameter and demonstrate a formulation-space-based strategy for comparing polymeric excipients without relying on a single predefined formulation composition.

item.title: Stability and Raman Spectra of Carbon Nanotube Fragments across Chirality and Length
item.description: Bare-ended carbon nanotube (CNT) fragments restructure at their rims. Geometry screening and density functional vibrational analysis identify 13 local minima on the restricted-singlet surface; six have stable restricted solutions. Energy per carbon, fitted to the inverse squared mean optimized diameter and separate initial armchair-like and zigzag-like rim fractions (R2 = 0.993), gives effective end coefficients of 2.12 and 2.64 eV per initial rim carbon, respectively. Eleven minima contain 58 short end pairs and 58 high-frequency, mainly collective pair-stretching modes. In three armchair minima with stable restricted solutions, the pair-stretch band rises from 1994–2016 cm−1 in (3,3) to 2046–2099 cm−1 in (5,5) as mean pair length falls from 1.235 to 1.228 Å; hydrogen capping of (3,3) lengthens the pairs to 1.338 Å and removes the band. With symmetry retained, capping removes all imaginary modes of (0,3) and (2,2) and reduces those of (0,4) from eight to two. Releasing symmetry yields minima with stable restricted solutions for all three. In five chiral minima, unrestricted solutions place nearly full, opposite spins on one isolated twocoordinate carbon per end. Selective capping stabilizes closed-shell (2,3) and retains the band. Unrestricted relaxation also retains it, with 4.14-fold lower total Raman activity than the restricted reference.

item.title: Phosphorus-Functionalized Carbon Quantum Dot-Doped Alginate Beads for Rapid and High-Capacity Recovery of Rare Earth Elements
item.description: Recovering rare earth elements (REEs) from waste streams requires adsorbents that combine rapid uptake, high capacity, and effective regeneration. Here, phosphorus-functionalized carbon quantum dots immobilized on alginate beads (P-CQD/ALG) were developed to integrate REE-binding functionality with a readily separable solid form. First, phosphorus functionalization (P-CQD/ALG) showed substantially higher Ce3+ removal than pristine alginate and unmodified or nitrogen-functionalized CQD composites, suggesting P-CQD/ALG as an optimal adsorbent. Second, P-CQD/ALG also achieved fast, strong, and selective removal of 11 REEs at 78%–95% after 60 min in synthetic solutions at pH 6.8, while uptake of most other common metals was ≤9%. One exception was that Fe3+ outcompeted most REEs, identifying the requirement for iron pre-treatment. Spectroscopic characterization and uptake trends suggest electrostatic attraction and coordination with phosphorus-containing oxygen groups as major mechanisms. Third, Langmuir adsorption capacities reached 301–430 mg/g for Ce3+ and Er3+, 1.1–36 times higher than the existing materials. The capacity-normalized cost (0.05–0.07 $/kg per mg/g) was also 7–3780 times lower than other materials. Lastly, dilute HNO3 (0.05 M) enabled Ce3+ desorption and repeated adsorption over five cycles. These findings identify P-CQD/ALG as a promising platform for REE recovery, with further validation needed in real wastewaters.

item.title: Divergent Synthesis of Diazaspiroalkanes through Spirolactam Intermediates
item.description: The use of spirocyclic diamines in molecular design requires both access to the desired framework and control over the nitrogen available for functionalization. We describe a divergent synthesis that addresses these requirements through common spirolactam intermediates. Starting from three commercially available methyl N-Boc cyclic amino esters, cyanoalkylation and nitrile reduction/lactamization afforded six frameworks. Two complementary benzyl/Boc sequences then delivered 11 mono-Boc diamines in final preparations of 1.8-25 g, including five pairs with opposite protection arrangements. This work extends established lactam-based chemistry across ring size, nitrogen connectivity, and protection site through a shared set of intermediates. The study also distinguishes limitations in pipecolate cyanoethylation, seven-membered lactam formation, and final debenzylation of one [3.6] derivative, which should guide selection of a productive route. Alongside the final diamines, the NH-containing lactams and monobenzyl intermediates provide additional points for molecular elaboration. Their preparative accessibility enables future studies of how changes in spirodiamine connectivity and attachment site affect the properties of more complex molecules.

item.title: Kinetic-thermodynamic symmetry breaking in reversible two-step polycondensation
item.description: Reversible step-growth polycondensation underpins the industrial manufacture of polyamides, polyesters and polycarbonates. Yet its classical Carothers–Flory description, built on Flory’s principle of equal reactivity and on a closed-system treatment, leaves a family of recurring process anomalies outside any single theoretical framework. Here we extend the asymmetric two-step pairing scheme of the companion theory with a reverse selectivity β and introduce an independent activity factor χ for the by-product (water), obtaining a closed-form, three-parameter theory of the equilibrium structure (Ω, K̂1 ≡ K1/χ; r), with Ω ≡ 4K2/K1 = 2α/β. Within the single three-parameter map, we relax both idealizations at once (equal reactivity and the closed system) and obtain closed forms for the equilibrium state: a cubic equation for the free A end-group concentration σ with a unique physical root, exact insensitivity to the rate-level asymmetry α (a catalyst changes the rate, never the equilibrium), and exact recovery of the Flory–Schulz most-probable distribution at Ω = 1. For the system under a time-dependent by-product activity we predict three falsifiable high-vacuum scaling laws, σ ∝ χ1/2, the total cyclic oligomer content ∝ χ1/2 and the residual monomer content ∝ χ, together with a three-regime scaling law for the dominant relaxation mode whose marginal branch at exact stoichiometry scales as χ−1/2. Each exponent can be obtained as the slope of a double-logarithmic plot from measurements that existing equipment can provide. Eight recurring process anomalies are mapped onto the parameters with explicitly graded evidence, and a single calibration point provides a reference point for the framework: the sealed-tube PA6 free end-group concentration σ ≈ 0.25 inverts in closed form to Ω ≈ 496. The framework thereby extends the Carothers–Flory paradigm from a closed, equal-reactivity idealization to the open, kinetically asymmetric regime in which industrial polycondensation actually operates.

item.title: Site-Selective Peripheral Aryl Substitution Tunes Red-to-Near-Infrared Fluorescence in Thienopyrazine-Fused Pyrene Heteroacenes
item.description: We report four thienopyrazine-fused pyrene heteroacenes with aryl substituents varied at the pyrene core and flanking thiophene rings. Compounds 1–3 exhibit neat-film photoluminescence quantum yields of 64–88% at 564–589 nm, whereas compound 4 displays an emission maximum at 767 nm in solution. Single-crystal analysis of 2 shows that cofacial p–p interactions between the central aromatic cores are impeded. The results show that both the position and identity of peripheral aryl substituents influence the photoluminescence properties of a common heteroacene framework.

item.title: Electronic versus magnetic descriptors of excited-state (anti)aromaticity: a critical assessment for singlet and triplet states
item.description: Excited-state aromaticity (ESA) and antiaromaticity (ESAA) are important concepts for understanding photochemical and photophysical processes. To quantify their extent and to follow ESA gain and ESAA relief, it would be beneficial to have aromaticity indices that are readily computable for higher excited states, applicable independently of the spin multiplicity, and suitable for non-equilibrium geometries. However, current aromaticity indices remain difficult to evaluate beyond the lowest triplet state and away from equilibrium structures. Within this work, we evaluate the feasibility of using electronic aromaticity indices (EAIs) derived from time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) as a lightweight and easily applicable measure of ES(A)A. The results are compared with complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) and DFT computations, considering both EAIs and nucleus-independent chemical shifts (NICS). Using para-quinodimethane, benzene, and naphthalene as test systems, we find qualitative agreement between EAIs computed with TDDFT and CASSCF. Comparing EAIs and NICS, we find agreement for the lowest triplet states, but opposing aromaticity/antiaromaticity assignments are obtained for the singlet states. Furthermore, NICS provide an intuitive picture of ESA gain and ESAA relief upon structural relaxation, whereas EAIs do not show this consistently. In summary, EAIs and NICS are both promising for quantifying ES(A)A, but clear pitfalls exist: both should be applied with care, and the meaning of (anti)aromaticity in higher, multiconfigurational excited states warrants further study.

item.title: Spatial arrangement of bonds governs the thermodynamics of multivalent DNA origami interfaces
item.description: Multivalency, the simultaneous engagement of many weak bonds, underlies recognition between cells, viruses, and proteins and enables assembly of DNA origami into micrometer-scale structures. Predicting the stability of a multivalent interface is difficult because each bond's contribution depends on the number, strength, and arrangement of the other bonds and on the scaffold that presents them, which rarely vary independently. We use DNA origami tiles with 11 addressable sites along one edge to build 236 interfaces in which bond number, strength, and arrangement are set independently, and measure their melting by FRET. Multivalency stabilizes interfaces far beyond any single bond. Once two tiles dock, each further bond finds its partner at an effective concentration about 105-fold above the tile concentration. Stability nevertheless grows subadditively, because only part of an interface melts as one unit and added bonds contribute only insofar as they are formed near the interface melting temperature. Arrangement matters as much as identity: interfaces built from the same bonds lose stability as bonds spread apart, and moving one bond away from two fixed bonds costs 2.5–3 °C per skipped site. A three-parameter multivalent model in which each bond’s effective concentration decays with its distance from the others predicts held-out melting temperatures to within 1.3 °C, outperforming a gradient-boosted regressor. Coarse-grained simulations of polymer-tethered binders reproduce this loss and show that linker and scaffold rigidity set how well binding sites stay in register. These results give design rules and a predictive tool for multicomponent DNA assembly and other multivalent systems.

item.title: Mechanism in Structure: Narrated and Interactive Tutorials on Hemoglobin and Chymotrypsin Built from Protein Data Bank Structures
item.description: Students usually meet an enzyme mechanism as a two-dimensional textbook figure and the enzyme itself as a separate threedimensional image, and the two rarely meet. This article describes two tutorials that place each mechanistic step in the real structure, beside a two-dimensional panel drawn after the course textbook. The hemoglobin tutorial follows the T→R transition: the iron moving into the heme plane, the rotation of one αβ dimer against the other, the ion pairs that break, the central cavity and the Bohr effect. The chymotrypsin tutorial follows the catalytic triad through acylation and deacylation, the oxyanion hole, burst kinetics and zymogen activation. Each tutorial is a narrated video in the instructor’s own voice (3 min 42 s and 5 min 12 s) and an interactive browser version with checkpoint questions, both built from one Unity scene, using seven Protein Data Bank entries in all. Scripts measured every distance, angle and rotation that the narration states. Most agree with the textbook, but one contact in its ion-pair figure, the Arg 141α carboxylate with Val1α′, is not an ion pair in three deoxyhemoglobin crystal structures, as was first noted when the structure was refined in 1975. The same hemoglobin request given to a commercial AI animation service returned accurate numbers, but no tie to the textbook and no record of its checks. The tutorials, scripts and reports are free and open; use in an undergraduate biochemistry course is planned for Fall 2027.

item.title: A Frontside SN2 Glycosylation Reaction
item.description: Understanding and controlling the stereochemical outcome of glycosylation reactions remains a fundamental challenge in synthetic carbohydrate chemistry. The SN1-SN2 reaction mechanism continuum is commonly employed to account for the stereochemistry of glycosylation reactions and to explain the reactivity of reactive intermediates. In this continuum, covalent anomeric triflates serve as glycosylating species in backside SN2 (SN2-b) pathways, and triflate ion – oxocarbenium ion pairs are central on the SN1-side of the spectrum. We here describe a frontside SN2-like (SN2-f) glycosylation reaction mechanism, in which an anomeric triflate is substituted with retention of configuration at the anomeric center by an incoming nucleophile. This unusual reaction mechanism bears strong resemblance to the mechanism employed by retaining glycosyl transferases in nature and benefits from a stabilizing hydrogen bond between the incoming nucleophile and triflate leaving group. In doing so, the nucleophilicity of the alcohol and leaving group capacity of the triflate are enhanced. The charge separation that develops in the transition state is optimally accommodated to allow for a low-energy reaction path in the apolar solvents that are employed in chemical glycosylation reactions. The reaction mechanism was discovered in the stereoretentive glycosylation reactions of 4,6-O-di-tert-butylsilylene (DTBS)-protected galactosyl triflates. Using 19F exchange spectroscopy (EXSY) NMR, 1H chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) NMR, kinetic isotope effect (KIE) measurements, and acceptor competition studies in combination with density functional theory (DFT) calculations and activation strain model (ASM) analysis the frontside SN2-reaction has been mapped. The hydrogen bonding interactions between the nucleophile and the triflate leaving group are revealed to stabilize the transition state and enhance the reactivity of electron poor nucleophiles to render them more reactive than their electron rich counterparts. Implementation of the SN2-f pathway in the continuum of glycosylation reaction mechanisms will enable the better understanding of glycosylation reaction outcomes and inspire the development of new stereoselective glycosylation methodology.

item.title: Relaxation-time analysis reveals resistance redistribution during selectivity oscillations in CO2-to-CO electrolysers
item.description: Selectivity oscillations between CO2 reduction and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) limit stable operation of membrane electrode assemblies, yet cell voltage and total impedance cannot identify their origin. We combine operando galvanostatic impedance spectroscopy, frequency band integration of the distribution of relaxation times (DRT), and a membrane reference strip to track recurrent transitions in an Ag CO2-to-CO electrolyser. Over 70 h, the coefficients of variation of the total resistance and the 0.1-2 Hz band resistance were 6.6% and approximately 40%, respectively. Each HER transition shifted resistance from the 20-250 Hz charge transfer response into slower 0.1-20 Hz CO2 transport responses, predominantly at the cathode, and incomplete recovery accumulated over successive cycles. The same metrics distinguished spontaneous transitions from imposed CO2 starvation, which produced the opposite shift, and showed that heating to 60 °C suppressed recurrent cycling at 10 and 50 mM KHCO3 while the cells approached HER-rich states. Hence, resolving where resistance redistributes within each cycle and how it accumulates between cycles provides a transferable operando diagnostic for unstable operation of CO2 electrolysers.

item.title: Deuteration as a General Strategy to Enhance Small Molecule-Based Photodynamic Therapy
item.description: Utilizing isotope effects has a long history in organic chemistry, and has recently been shown to improve fluorophore photophysics and azobenzene-based photoswitch kinetics. Herein, we report the deuteration of methylene blue (MB) and sulfonated tetraphenyl porphyrin (TPPS), both far-red singlet oxygen sensitizers (SOSs), which boosts the efficiency of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by >55%. We applied this knowledge to photodynamic therapeutic (PDT) settings by derivatizing deuterated methylene blue as 1) a ligand for the HaloTag protein (HTP) that leads to faster activation kinetics of the ROS-sensitive TRAAK channel, 2) as a fusion to a peptidic agonist of the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP1R) to optically induce ablation of GLP1R-expressing cells, and 3) as a lysosome targeting sensitizer to induce spatiotemporally controlled lysosomal damage through lipid oxidation. Taken together, our strategy provides a simple way to improve well-studied singlet oxygen sensitizers through deuteration and leverages the best performing sensitizer across a set of different biological methodologies to study ion channel gating, as well as organelle and cell ablation.

item.title: Functionalized 2-Substituted Oxetanes through Epoxide Ring Expansion
item.description: The value of an oxetane building block depends on access to both its substitution pattern and a functional group that can be modified without consuming the ring. We examined the Corey-Chaykovsky ring expansion of alcohol-derived epoxides as an entry to functionalized 2-substituted oxetanes. Benzyl-protected allylic alcohols provided precursors for varying side-chain branching and substitution at the future C2 center. Productive expansion favored terminal epoxides, whereas substitution at both epoxide carbons strongly restricted oxetane formation and could lead to products consistent with epoxide-to-allylic-alcohol isomerization. Commercial enantiopure epoxides gave both enantiomeric oxetanylmethanol series while preserving the enantiomeric excess. The resulting alcohols were converted into primary and secondary amines, halides, ketones, and a carboxylic acid on multigram scales. The model alcohol was isolated in a single 403 g batch. Extension to homoallylic alcohols gave access to a complementary two-carbon side-chain series, including aminoethyl and iodoethyl derivatives and lithium 2-(oxetan-2-yl)acetate. These results connect precursor topology, stereochemical transfer, and downstream functionalization in a preparative approach to related oxetane building blocks.

item.title: Double-hybrid quality reactivity in converged quantum environments at GGA-like speed: comparing local correlation and local quantum embedding accelerations
item.description: Double-hybrid (DH) density functionals provide the highest rung of DFT accuracy, but their MP2-like term can be computationally prohibitive, when including realistic chemical environments. Here, we extend our local embedded subsystem (LESS) framework, previously introduced for projector- and Huzinaga-equation-based quantum embedding for hybrid DFT-in-GGA, by implementing DH-in-DFT embedding with hybrid or GGA DFT environments. We also combine it with local MP2 (LMP2) and local DH (LDH) acceleration and analyze the performance of the resulting LDH-in-GGA and LESS-accelerated LDH-in-GGA variants compared to LESS DH-in-GGA. Benchmarks are reported for environment-inclusive organo-, enzymatic, and zeolite-catalyzed reactions (171–238 QM atoms), all exhibiting high DFT uncertainties at lower rungs. The LESS acceleration retains only 50–60% of the atomic orbital and 20–40% of the density-fitting basis functions for the high-level DH part, while yields uncertainties of only about 0.1 kcal/mol. Combined with mixed basis sets, LESS DH-in-GGA surpasses the speed of LMP2-based LDH for these realistic environment sizes, requiring 4-8 core hours, i.e., two orders of magnitude speedup over conventional DH DFT. Importantly, the cost of the DH part in LESS DH-in-DFT becomes comparable or less than the full system low-level DFT computation, even with GGA environment models. Our additional motivation emerges from the lower complexity of LESS Huzinaga embedding from the perspective of implementing derivative and spectroscopic properties. This technical benefit, in combination with its outstanding accuracy-over-cost performance, makes LESS-based quantum embedding highly competitive with local correlation as a route to enable DH quality simulations at routine cost, with proper chemical environments.

item.title: Heterostructured BiVO4/g-C3N4 Semiconductor Nanomaterials for Enhanced Visible-Light-Driven Degradation and Mineralization of Emerging Water Contaminants
item.description: The persistence of emerging contaminants (ECs)—including pharmaceuticals, endocrine-disrupting compounds, and synthetic dyes—in aquatic ecosystems poses a critical threat to environmental and public health due to their resistance to conventional wastewater treatment processes. Semiconductor photocatalysis offers a sustainable, solar-driven pathway for complete pollutant mineralization, yet single-component photocatalysts suffer from rapid electron–hole recombination and limited visible-light utilization. In this study, we report the rational design and synthesis of a two-dimensional/three-dimensional (2D/3D) Z-scheme heterostructured bismuth vanadate/graphitic carbon nitride (BiVO4/g-C3N4) nanocomposite via a facile hydrothermal–calcination coupling strategy. Structural and morphological characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) confirms the intimate interfacial contact between monoclinic scheelite BiVO4 nanoparticles and ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets. Optical and photoelectrochemical analyses—including UV–Vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS), photoluminescence (PL), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)—demonstrate extended visible-light harvesting up to 540 nm, suppressed charge-carrier recombination, and accelerated interfacial charge transfer. Under simulated visible-light irradiation (λ ≥ 420 nm), the optimized 15 wt% BiVO4/g-C3N4 heterojunction achieved 96.4% degradation of tetracycline hydrochloride within 90 min, exhibiting an apparent pseudo-first-order rate constant (k = 0.0368 min-1) that is 4.3-fold and 5.8-fold higher than pristine g-C3N4 and bare BiVO4, respectively. Total organic carbon (TOC) analysis confirmed 81.2% mineralization efficiency, while radical scavenging and electron spin resonance (ESR) experiments verified that superoxide (•O2-) and hydroxyl (•OH) radicals serve as the primary reactive oxidative species, substantiating a direct Z-scheme charge-transfer mechanism. Furthermore, the composite retained greater than 91% of its catalytic activity over five consecutive recycling runs, demonstrating strong structural stability for practical water remediation.

item.title: [HYD-Py]3: light- and acid-driven reversible in-plane ring breathing between physicochemically and functionally distinct expanded and contracted states of an 18-membered nonaazamacrocycle
item.description: Stimuli-responsive macrocycles can alter shape through conformational reorganization or changes in covalent connectivity, but repeatable, connectivity-preserving resizing of an intact ring has remained elusive. Here we report [HYD-Py]3, an 18-membered nonaazamacrocycle that undergoes reversible in-plane ring breathing while preserving atom count and bonding topology. Condition-selective divergent cyclotrimerization of a bifunctional pyridine monomer furnishes expanded all-trans and contracted all-cis states, the latter locked by a cyclic array of three intramolecular N–H···N hydrogen bonds. Irradiation drives contraction via sequential C=N isomerization within the intact macrocyclic skeleton, whereas trifluoroacetic acid disrupts the hydrogen-bond network and restores the expanded state, enabling repeated cycling. Ring breathing reconfigures cavity size and surface polarity, producing distinct solubility, fluorescence, self-association propensities and π-surface recognition; the expanded state also functions as a multidentate metal-ion receptor.

item.title: MeCoBi: Fast and accurate 3D metal complex structures for structure-based machine learning
item.description: The three-dimensional arrangement of ligands around a metal centre determines its electronic structure, reactivity, and biological activity, yet generating accurate 3D structures from a string-based input remains difficult. Existing tools are slow, narrow in coverage, or need the coordination environment to be specified by hand. We present MeCoBi (Metal Complex Builder), an automated pipeline that builds and optimises 3D structures of mononuclear metal complexes from ligand SMILES across 36 d-block and main-group metals and coordination numbers 2–9. On 30,830 experimental structures from the Cambridge Structural Database, MeCoBi generated a structure for 99.6% of complexes with a median error in metal–ligand bond lengths of 0.06 Å. Used as machine-learning inputs, these structures ranked the untested members of an in-house library of 1,800 iridium complexes at least as well as the best 2D models (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.88 against at most 0.86); and, through GFN2-xTB single points, lowered the error of a two-dimensional model for the dipole moments and HOMO–LUMO gaps of 10,175 tmQM complexes from 1.68 to 1.24 D and from 0.367 to 0.311 eV. MeCoBi is open source, with a web interface at mecobi.york.ac.uk.

item.title: Chemically specific NMR relaxation in thermally modified mesoporous materials
item.description: Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) relaxation provides a non-invasive method for characterising solid–liquid interactions within porous materials. However, the influence of pore surface chemistry on the surface relaxivity of different liquid adsorbates remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the effects of thermal surface modification on eight liquid adsorbates (cyclohexane, acetone and six alcohols) confined within mesoporous silicas and γ-alumina using low-field (12.7 MHz) two-dimensional 1H T1–T2 relaxation measurements. Thermal treatment reduced the T1/T2 ratios of the alkyl groups of confined alcohols, indicating reduced surface affinity, with the magnitude of this reduction dependent on alcohol structure. Furthermore, by examining cyclohexane, acetone and methanol confined within mesoporous silicas with nominal pore sizes between 6 and 50 nm, we quantify, for the first time, the influence of surface dehydroxylation on both longitudinal and transverse surface relaxivities. Silica pore surface dehydroxylation reduced the transverse surface relaxivities of acetone and both functional groups of methanol by approximately 40–60%, whereas that of cyclohexane remained nearly unchanged. Overall, these findings demonstrate the sensitivity of nuclear spin surface relaxivity to both adsorbate chemistry and pore surface functionalisation, and highlight the potential of low-field NMR relaxation for characterising surface chemistry changes in functional porous materials.

item.title: Molecular Controls of Doping-Induced Chain Stiffness in Conjugated Polymers
item.description: Electronic doping planarizes conjugated polymer backbones and enhances quinoidal character, but its effects on chain-scale conformations relevant to packing, orientation, and charge transport remain poorly understood. Predicting these effects is challenging because electronic delocalization and backbone rotation are nonlocally coupled. Here, we develop a coarse-grained tight-binding molecular dynamics model that incorporates nonlocal electronic contributions to backbone rotational forces to predict dopingdependent conjugation and persistence lengths. Parameterized using density functional theory for polythiophene derivatives, the model captures charged-state conformational energetics more accurately than independent torsional potentials. Simulations and systematic parameter scans reveal distinct molecular controls: electronic coupling and neutral-state torsional minima govern conjugation, whereas backbone deflection angles and relative stabilities of planar conformers determine chain persistence. Consequently, doping increases conjugation while producing strongly chemistry-dependent changes in chain stiffness, including persistence-length increases approaching 500%. These findings establish molecular design principles for controlling the chain-scale structural response to doping.

item.title: The Nature of Protein Hierarchies and Implications for Hierarchical Modelling: An AI-Assisted Computational Study with Statistical Mechanics, Information Theory and Unsupervised Learning
item.description: Proteins are widely described as hierarchies of nested structural units, and hierarchical models are widely used to simulate them, yet what kind of hierarchy proteins actually possess, and what that hierarchy implies for how they should be modelled, has not been established. This work addresses these two questions directly. It builds on three earlier studies from this laboratory, on foldability of lattice proteins, on the relationship between folding and function, and on elastic network models (GNM and ANM) of real proteins, which established hierarchical modularity but left its physical nature and modelling consequences open. Using statistical mechanics (exactly solvable hierarchical foldon models, lattice simulations, residue-level folding ensembles and harmonic elastic networks), an information-theoretic approach (tree decomposition of total correlation, mutual information and exact free-energy cycles) and unsupervised learning (variational autoencoders), and calibrating every index against compact-polymer nulls, matched alternative trees, optimized flat partitions and a frozen protocol on reserved protein families, we find that the hierarchy of proteins is mechanical and organizational rather than thermodynamic. Native contact networks have reproducible, sequence-local nested modules, but nesting itself is shared with compact polymers. item.title: Engineering Stable and Targeted NIR/SWIR Imaging Agents through Metal-Organic Framework Nanoconfinement
item.description: Near-infrared (NIR) and shortwave infrared (SWIR) fluorophores offer significant potential for biomedical imaging owing to their deep tissue penetration and low background autofluorescence. However, their widespread application remains limited by poor aqueous solubility, aggregation-induced fluorescence loss, and inadequate stability in physiological environments. Here, we present a general nanoconfinement strategy that converts hydrophobic molecular fluorophores into stable, bright, and engineerable imaging nanocomposites through encapsulation within the large-pore metal-organic framework ZIF-71. Using IR-780 as a model dye and extending the approach to the larger fluorophores IR-813 and IR-1048, we demonstrate that in situ encapsulation preserves a predominantly monomeric dye population within the ZIF-71 framework, effectively suppressing aggregation across diverse aqueous environments, including physiologically relevant and high-salinity conditions. Compared with free dyes and benchmark micellar formulations, the IR-780@ZIF composites exhibit markedly improved resistance to aggregation, enhanced solution and photostability, and substantially increased fluorescence quantum yields and imaging brightness in water and phosphate-buffered saline. The benefits of confinement become increasingly pronounced for larger and more hydrophobic fluorophores, turning essentially dark free dyes IR-813 and IR-1048 in aqueous media into bright composites. Importantly, the external surface of the ZIF particles can be modified orthogonally through post-synthetic functionalization without compromising the optical properties of the encapsulated fluorophore. Surface incorporation of biotin and cell-penetrating peptide ligands enables tailored cellular delivery of the fluorophores, demonstrating the modularity of the platform. Collectively, these results establish large-pore ZIFs as versatile hosts for molecular NIR/SWIR fluorophores and highlight MOF nanoconfinement as a powerful strategy for integrating high-performance photophysics with customizable biological functionality for advanced imaging applications.

item.title: Radical Sorting Enables Semiconductor-Driven Redox-Neutral C(sp3)–C(sp3) Cross-Coupling
item.description: Selective formation of C(sp3)–C(sp3) bonds from carbon-centered radicals is inherently challenging, because competing radical homocoupling can compromise product selectivity. Here, we combine heterogeneous semiconductor photocatalysis with nickel-mediated radical sorting to achieve redox-neutral C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation. Under irradiation, graphitic carbon nitride (gCN) generates alkyl radicals from carboxylic acids and redox-active esters (RAEs) through complementary oxidative and reductive single-electron transfer, respectively, without the need for stoichiometric oxidants or reductants. A nickel catalyst channels these intermediates towards cross-coupling, providing access to a range of products bearing primary and secondary alkyl fragments, including saturated heterocycles, unnatural amino acids, and late-stage functionalization products. Kinetic modelling, radical-clock experiments, electrochemical measurements, and DFT calculations provide insight into the origin of radical sorting. The results are consistent with sequential radical capture at nickel and identify the suppression of homocoupling between RAE-derived radicals as a key kinetic feature.

item.title: From Divergence to Coupling: Interfacial Water and Adsorbed Hydrogen during Hydrogen Evolution
item.description: The structure of interfacial water is widely invoked to explain the kinetics of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet how it evolves relative to adsorbed hydrogen (H*) and responds to changes in electrode potential remains unclear. Here, we simultaneously track interfacial water and H* on platinum during potential pulses using Dynamic Response Spectroscopy (DRS), which separates interfacial-and diffusion-layer contributions to the measured spectra. As the potential is lowered from 0.4 VRHE, we identify three potential regions, defined by the dominant interfacial processes and characterized by different relationships between water and H* dynamics. In the hydrogen underpotential deposition region, where H* adsorption dominates, H* follows each potential step, whereas interfacial water restructures progressively over the first cycles and does not recover its initial configuration. At 0 VRHE, where hydrogen adsorption and evolution are in equilibrium, water follows each potential step but continues to relax during holds at constant H* coverage. Under net HER, water and H* evolve in concert. These results show that hydrogen coverage alone does not determine the dynamic state of interfacial water. Rather, their dynamic coupling depends on the dominant interfacial process, highlighting the importance of interfacial history when interpreting spectroscopic measurements of electrocatalytic interfaces.

item.title: Apparent Recovery Reverses Healing-Rate Rankings Among Soft Polymers
item.description: Abstract Autonomous self-healing at room temperature can extend polymer lifetimes, but combining rapid healing with mechanical robustness remains challenging. Tensile toughness recovery is widely used to compare polymers and infer healing mechanisms. However, the chain mobility enabling healing also permits large bulk deformation and stress redistribution during testing, masking residual interfacial weakness. This polymer-dependent apparent recovery can be so pronounced that the ranking of healing rates inferred from toughness recovery becomes opposite to that of interfacial mechanical recovery. To reduce this masking, tensile testing at the lower boundary of the glass-transition region is combined with inverse finiteelement analysis. Using the inferred interfacial states, upper-boundary simulations distinguish interfacial and bulk contributions to macroscopic tensile behavior, explaining the observed ranking reversal. These findings show that conventional room-temperature tensile toughness recovery can mislead both comparisons of self-healing performance and interpretations of its governing mechanisms. With masking reduced, interfacial mechanical recovery proves much slower than conventional toughness-recovery measurements suggest, and its ranking cannot be explained by bulk softness alone. In contrast, macroscopic crack closure proceeds far more rapidly and is governed largely by chain mobility. Tailoring interchain interactions to accelerate the rate-limiting interfacial reconstruction may reconcile rapid healing with mechanical robustness without further bulk softening.

item.title: Solvent-Directed Heat Shock for Engineering Emissive States in Nonconjugated Polymers: Towards Single-Component Cool-White Light Emission
item.description: Non-conjugated polymers can be engineered into highly photoluminescent materials without conventional πconjugated chromophores by activating their through-space electronic states. However, the development of a low-energy cluster-state emitter from a simple polymer without chemical modification remains a fundamental challenge. We report here a solvent-directed heat-shock approach that reconfigures the excited-state landscape of the water-soluble, biocompatible, carbonyl-rich pharmaceutical binder polymer poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (weak high-energy emitter). Ethanol is used as a transient chain-mobilizing medium: rotary evaporation redistributes and pre-associates the pendant carbonyls within a viscous, solvent-dried film, and heating just above the ethanol boiling point removes the residual solvent and collapses the swollen matrix into a rigid cluster state. The rigid clusters display strong visible clusteroluminescence (350-750 nm) upon excitation with longwavelength UV and visible light, yielding single-component cool white emission (CIE 0.26, 0.33) under 405 nm excitation. The retained cool-white emission in aqueous media across the 1-30 mg mL-1 concentration range expands this approach beyond dry solids, linking nonconventional photophysics to water-processable soft materials.

item.title: Thermodynamic Model of Mixing and Photo-Demixing in MAPb(I,Br)3 from Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
item.description: Mixed-halide lead perovskites are promising materials for solar cells because of high photoconversion efficiencies and bandgaps that can be finely tuned through composition, but their application is limited by reversible light-induced halide segregation. Here, we investigate the thermodynamic origin of the segregation behaviour in MAPb(I,Br)3 by combining molecular dynamics, based on a machine-learned interatomic potential fine-tuned to r2SCAN density-functional-theory data, with a model for the electronic and elastic contributions that arise under illumination. The simulations give the free energy of mixing in the dark across the full composition range, including configurational and molecular rotational effects. Our results indicate that the mixed material is thermodynamically stable in the dark at 350 K and, by extrapolation, at room temperature, in contrast with earlier theoretical predictions of a room-temperature miscibility gap and consistent with the spontaneous remixing observed once illumination is removed. Under illumination, the accumulation of photocarriers in lower-bandgap iodide-rich regions favours compositional separation. Within this band-gap model, the carrier density at which incipient iodide-rich domains become thermodynamically favourable is within the range of 1-sun illumination for Br-rich alloys, but forming a macroscopic iodide-rich phase that occupies a few percent of the material, with the observed composition, requires carrier densities about four orders of magnitude higher. The more stable dark free energy obtained here widens this gap, and incorporating the coherency strain between the phases into the model widens it further. These results indicate that the band-gap model accounts only for the onset of photo-demixing and not for its macroscopic stage, which must involve additional physics, and demonstrate that reliable models of photo-demixing require an accurate, dynamic description of the dark thermodynamics.

item.title: Copper-Mediated Bromodeboronation of Alkenyl Pinacol Boronates: Scope and Stereochemical Outcome
item.description: A practical approach to functionalized alkenyl bromides based on CuBr2-mediated bromodeboronation of alkenyl pinacol boronates was developed. The target products were obtained in THF/H2O (10:1) at 70 °C in 35–90% yield from acyclic as well as four- to seven-membered carbocyclic and heterocyclic precursors. The reaction was compatible with N-Boc-protected amines, ethers, sulfones, fluorinated groups, esters, and a free carboxylic acid and could be performed on a multigram scale. Flexible boronates bearing pendant nucleophilic groups and an allylic bromide were not tolerated. The starting isomer composition and geometry were generally preserved, with limited substrate-dependent changes. In a direct comparison with NBS and Br2/NaOMe on representative substrates, CuBr2 gave higher yields for most of them.
